description: High school students interested in engineering, space, and artificial intelligence research. Experience in competitive robotics and independent research.
summary: Ground Station makes convoluted NASA Earth data accessible and digestible for people of all backgrounds. Our interactive globe allows users to easily select their desired location and instantly receive trends and measurements for environmental variables. Each result shows its source, units and dates. Users can compare measurements and export the data as CSV. Users can see how confident we are in each long-term trend and the statistical evidence for it. We pulled the data from GPM IMERG, MERRA-2, GLDAS and AIRS using NASA Giovanni. Although powerful, Giovanni is hard to navigate for the average user, so we designed this project to make its data as intuitive to access as possible. For policy makers, it gives them clear insight about the climate situation in their country, which is especially useful in a crisis. For farmers, it gives them local rainfall and soil moisture patterns to plan when to plant. For student researchers, it gives them easy access to decades of data. Everybody deserves the right to understand our world, and the first step is giving them the data to do so.
details:
What does it do?

Ground Station takes NASA's extensive and complex Earth data accessible and digestible for everyone. Users select a location on our interactive globe and are able to instantly see how variables have changed, by how much, and statistical significance.

  • Explore 15 variables encompassing land, water and air:
    • Land: air and surface temperature, rainfall, humidity, root-zone soil moisture, evaporation, wind and snow.
    • Water: sea-surface temperature, air temperature and rainfall over the ocean.
    • Air: ozone, water vapour, cloud fraction, tropopause temperature and outgoing longwave radiation.
    • Annual, monthly and monthly anomaly graphs.
    • Change per decade, 95% confidence interval, and trend (rising, falling, no trend).
    • Each statistic is explained simply when hovered over.
    • Lag of up to six months.
  • Read relevant regional news and research.
  • Export the data, trends, forecast and methods as CSV files with sources and units.

How does it work?
Data collection: we used the NASA Giovanni API, with Earthdata authentication, to download monthly records for about 7,000 locations sampled roughly 3° apart. The sources are GPM IMERG (rainfall), MERRA-2 (air temperature, humidity, ozone, tropopause), GLDAS 2.0 (soil moisture, evaporation, snow, wind, surface temperature) and AIRS (water vapour, clouds, outgoing radiation, sea-surface temperature). Storage: the records are stored in a Supabase (PostgreSQL) database, so the globe loads them instantly. A refresh function can fetch new entries from Giovanni and NASA’s CMR catalogue. Trend analysis: each year is averaged to remove the seasons. A least-squares line gives the change per decade. Newey–West standard errors account for years that depend on each other. The Mann–Kendall test with the Hamed–Rao correction gives an independent second check, with a Theil–Sen slope as a robust rate. Holm correction protects the panel and Benjamini–Hochberg protects the map against false positives from running many tests at once. Interface: a WebGL globe with custom shaders to render the heatmaps, the country selections and the comparison maps in the browser.

What benefits does it have?

The data is already openly published by NASA. However, using it requires sifting through thousands of points, understanding coverage, units, and configuring plots. That barrier to entry deters most people without technical backgrounds from even trying. Ground Station makes data accessible by starting with their questions and working back from there.

  • Basic trend analysis takes one click, no setup needed.
  • The app clarifies when a change isn't distinguishable from normal variations.
  • Every result and export will list the source, date, and units.
  • Students, journalists, or other interested users can easily integrate the numbers into their own work.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to democratise climate data. One example is Baidoa, Somalia. The 2010–12 food emergency in southern and central Somalia caused an estimated 258,000 excess deaths, about half of them being children under five. At a NASA rainfall point near Baidoa, the annual chart doesn't show a clear trend. After switching to monthly anomalies, two failed rainy seasons appear in 2010–11 showing 62% less rain than usual. Both seasons ended months before the Bay Region was declared in famine. Ground Station can make warning signs like this visible to anyone. The same workflow serves many users:

  • People checking if a dry season was unusual.
  • Policymakers screening where conditions are changing.
  • Farmers comparing rainfall with root-zone soil moisture.
  • Fishermen tracking sea-surface temperature.
  • Students exporting real NASA data.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Programming languages: JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, HTML5, CSS3, GLSL (WebGL shaders), SQL.
  • Front end: custom WebGL globe renderer and canvas charts, with no framework, built as static site.
  • Back end: Supabase (PostgreSQL database, REST API, and Edge Functions on Deno) for data refresh, AI assistant, research links and news.
  • Data pipeline: Python scripts for the NASA Giovanni API and Earthdata Login, and NASA CMR Search for granule discovery.
  • AI assistant: a large language model accessed through the Groq API. It can turn place questions into selections, and every statistic still comes from stored NASA data.
  • Geography: Natural Earth (countries, provinces, cities), RESOLVE Ecoregions 2017, the Open-Meteo Geocoding API and GeoNames.
  • News and research: The Guardian Open Platform, the GDELT Project, Google News links and OpenAlex.
  • Development tools: Git, GitHub, VS Code, Node.js (automated tests), Python’s http.server, and AI coding assistants (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex).

What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific validity:
    • We dropped GLDAS 2.1 from the trends because changes to its inputs create false warming.
    • We detected and masked a Greenland artifact, where NASA’s land model has no glacier physics and piles up snow forever.
    • We grade the forecast only on unseen years and places.
  • Statistical honesty: we correct for year-to-year correlation and for multiple testing, and we label every limit, including straight-line trends and short records.
  • Accessibility: plain-language labels, hover explanations, keyboard shortcuts, a help panel and a mobile layout.
  • Responsible framing: the app shows historical evidence and associations, not causes or disaster predictions. News is clearly separated from the data.
  • Openness: every result can be traced to its NASA source and exported for reuse.
